Archive item 1: AGEP Operations Handbook – Section 1: Facility Overview and Commissioning
Source format: Operations Handbook

This handbook provides the standard operating procedures, facility specifications, and safety protocols for the Aravalli Green Energy Park (hereafter "AGEP" or "the Park"). It is intended for all AGEP staff, contract personnel, and authorised visitors. Sections are numbered for ease of reference; any conflict between this handbook and a specific work order must be brought to the attention of the Facilities Manager.

**2. FACILITY IDENTIFICATION**

- **Facility Name:** Aravalli Green Energy Park (AGEP)
- **Registered Address:** Plot No. 7, Sector 18, Gurugram – 122015, Haryana, India
- **Land Area:** 12.5 acres
- **Total Built-Up Area:** 18,700 sq. m. (approx.)
- **Number of Main Blocks:** 3 (Admin Block, Operations Block, Maintenance Block)
- **Number of Floors:** Admin Block – 4 floors; Operations Block – 2 floors; Maintenance Block – single storey
- **Primary Function:** Solar energy generation, battery storage, and grid load balancing; also houses the regional dispatch office.

**3. COMMISSIONING RECORD**

The AGEP was formally commissioned on 15-04-2018, following the completion of Phase I construction and the successful run of the Standard Testing Procedure (STP) for all major subsystems. This date is recorded as the official commissioning date in the AGEP Operations Handbook and is used for all warranty, insurance, and statutory compliance calculations.

The commissioning certificate (Ref. No. AGEP/COMM/2018/01) is held in the Facilities Department filing cabinet (Cabinet 2, Drawer A). A copy is also available in the digital archive under "Legal & Compliance".

**4. MAJOR SYSTEMS OVERVIEW**

The AGEP Operations Handbook states that the commissioning_date of Aravalli Green Energy Park is 2018-04-15. Record status: current.

The following systems are critical to the Park's operation. Detailed maintenance schedules are in Section 5 of this handbook.

**4.1 Solar PV Array**
- **Capacity:** 8.5 MWp (DC), 7.2 MW (AC)
- **Module Type:** Monocrystalline, 330 Wp each
- **Inverter Count:** 24 (central string inverters, 300 kW each)
- **Mounting:** Fixed tilt at 24°, south-facing; ground-mounted in rows 1–6.

**4.2 Battery Energy Storage System (BESS)**
- **Capacity:** 10 MWh (lithium-ion)
- **Container Location:** North-east corner, behind Maintenance Block
- **Fire Suppression:** Dedicated aerosol-based system; do not enter BESS area without authorisation.

**4.3 HVAC System**
- **Admin Block:** Two 40 TR variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems; chiller backup of 50 TR.
- **Operations Block:** One 25 TR VRF system.
- **Maintenance Block:** Split AC units (3 units, 1.5 TR each) – not connected to central system.
- **Control Setpoint:** 24°C ± 1°C during occupied hours; 28°C during unoccupied hours (except server room, which is 22°C ± 2°C).

**4.4 Lighting**
- **Type:** LED throughout; 4000K colour temperature in office areas, 5000K in inspection bays.
- **Control:** Occupancy sensors in corridors and restrooms; daylight harvesting in open-plan offices.
- **Emergency Lighting:** Battery-backed units on each floor near stairwells; test weekly (see Section 7.4).

**4.5 Backup Power**
- **Diesel Generators (DG):** 2 × 500 kVA, auto-start on mains failure. One is on standby at all times.
- **Fuel Storage:** 2 × 10,000 litre underground tanks. Fuel quality tested quarterly as per IS 1460.
- **Changeover Time:** < 15 seconds via automatic transfer switch (ATS).

**4.6 Water Systems**
- **Source:** Borewell + municipal supply (dual feed).
- **STP:** On-site sewage treatment plant (STP) of 50 kLD capacity. Treated water used for landscaping and cooling tower make-up.
- **Cooling Tower:** 1 × 100 TR, induced draft, located on Admin Block roof.
**5.0 Daily Operations and Seasonal Adjustments**

The Park operates on a two-shift pattern for core maintenance and security staff, with administrative functions following standard office hours. Shift timings are as follows:

| Shift | Timings | Remarks |
|--------|---------|---------|
| General Shift (Admin) | 09:00 – 18:00 hrs | Monday to Saturday; second Saturday closed |
| Shift A (Operations) | 08:00 – 20:00 hrs | Rotating, 6 days on / 2 days off |
| Shift B (Operations) | 20:00 – 08:00 hrs | Rotating, 6 days on / 2 days off |
| Security | 24 × 7 | Three shifts of 8 hours each |

During Diwali and Holi weeks, the Admin Block follows a reduced schedule (10:00 – 16:00 hrs) unless prior approval is obtained from the Facility Manager for extended hours. The same applies to the week between Christmas and New Year. All leave requests during these periods must be submitted at least 15 days in advance.

**5.1 HVAC Scheduling**

The HVAC systems shall be operated according to the following schedule, which is reviewed quarterly and revised as needed:

| Zone | Occupied Hours | Unoccupied Hours | Notes |
|------|----------------|------------------|-------|
| Admin Block – VRF | 08:30 – 18:30 hrs | 28°C setpoint | Pre-cooling starts at 08:00 hrs |
| Admin Block – Chiller backup | Only when VRF under maintenance or ambient > 38°C | – | Changeover log to be maintained |
| Operations Block – VRF | 07:30 – 20:30 hrs | 28°C setpoint | Shift B has access to local override |
| Server Room (Admin Block) | 24 × 7 | 22°C ± 2°C | Redundant unit; alarm on high temp |
| Maintenance Block – Split Units | As per work requirement | OFF | Units to be switched off when bay is empty |

Seasonal adjustments: From 15 March to 15 October (summer period), the pre-cooling start time is advanced by 30 minutes in the Admin Block. During the monsoon (June to September), the VRF systems in the Operations Block shall be operated in dry mode whenever relative humidity exceeds 80%, as per the manufacturer's recommendation.

The chiller backup shall be started only with the prior approval of the Shift In-charge, and the reason for start-up must be recorded in the HVAC log register. Energy consumption for the chiller is tracked separately under the head "Chiller – Backup".

**5.2 Lighting Control**

Lighting schedules are programmed into the Building Management System (BMS) as follows:

- **Office areas (Admin Block):** 08:00 – 18:30 hrs, with daylight harvesting active. If lux level falls below 300 lux during overcast conditions, the system automatically raises artificial lighting to 50% and then to 100% if required.
- **Corridors and restrooms:** Occupancy sensors; time delay of 10 minutes after last detection.
- **Inspection bays (Maintenance Block):** Manual switching only. Bay lights shall be switched off when the bay is vacant. The last person leaving the bay shall verify all switches are off.
- **External lighting:** Dusk-to-dawn sensors on all pole-mounted fixtures. Perimeter lights remain ON throughout the night; decorative lighting near the entrance is on a timer from 19:00 to 06:00 hrs.
- **Parking area:** 50% lighting between 23:00 and 05:00 hrs to save energy, except in the designated CCTV-monitored zone where full lighting is maintained.

During daytime, all internal lights in unoccupied cabins shall be kept off. Housekeeping staff have been instructed to report any lights left on after 20:00 hrs to the Security Control Room, and the same is logged for the Facility Manager's morning review.

**5.3 Routine Inspections**

Daily, weekly, and monthly inspections are to be carried out as per the matrices below. The responsible person shall tick and sign the respective checklist; any abnormality must be reported immediately to the Shift In-charge.
## 6. SAFETY PROTOCOLS AND EMERGENCY PROCEDURES

### 6.1 General Safety Policy

AGEP is committed to providing a safe working environment for all employees, contractors, and visitors. Every person entering the facility shall comply with the safety rules outlined in this section and with applicable provisions of the Factories Act, 1948, and the Maharashtra Factories Rules, 1963. The Facility Manager is the designated Safety Officer for the premises and shall be responsible for the implementation of this policy.

Safety is everybody's responsibility. Any person noticing an unsafe condition, a potential hazard, or a near-miss incident shall report the same immediately to the Shift In-charge or to the Security Control Room (extension 101). Anonymous reporting is permitted through the suggestion box located near the main entrance gate. Reports received through this channel are reviewed by the Facility Manager on a weekly basis.

All employees shall undergo a safety induction before they are issued access cards. The induction covers fire safety, electrical safety, first aid, and emergency evacuation procedures. Contractors working on-site shall attend a condensed version of this induction, and their supervisor shall sign an acknowledgement confirming that the contractor staff have understood the rules. No contractor shall commence work without this acknowledgement on record.

### 6.2 Emergency Contact Numbers

The following numbers shall be prominently displayed on notice boards in every block, near all telephones, and inside each lift lobby. The list is reviewed quarterly and updated as and when personnel change. Please verify the list periodically and report any discrepancy to the Security Control Room.

| 11 | Ambulance (Private) | Lifeline Services | 022-2541-9988 |
| 12 | Nearest Hospital (Krishna Hospital) | Casualty | 022-2541-4455 |

The Security Control Room is manned round the clock. In case of an emergency occurring outside normal working hours, the control room operator shall contact the Facility Manager or, in his absence, the Deputy Facility Manager. The contact numbers of all shift personnel are available in the Security Control Room register and in the emergency contact directory maintained at the main gate.

### 6.3 Fire Safety Measures

#### 6.3.1 Fire Detection and Alarm System

The facility is equipped with an automatic fire detection and alarm system comprising smoke detectors, heat detectors, and manual call points. The system is connected to the BMS and to the Security Control Room. Activation of any detector or manual call point shall cause the alarm bells to ring in the affected zone and the adjacent zones, and the fire alarm panel shall indicate the zone of activation.

The fire alarm system is tested every Wednesday at 10:00 hrs by the Electrical Maintenance team. During the test, the alarm bells shall ring for a duration of not more than 30 seconds. Employees need not evacuate during the test. Any malfunction observed during the test shall be rectified within the same day.

Archive item 3: AGEP Equipment Manuals – Central Chiller Plant Technical Specifications
Source format: Equipment Manuals

The Central Chiller Plant (CCP), designated as Asset ENT10 in the campus asset register, is the primary source of chilled water for the air-conditioning system serving the administration block, central library, and the R&D wing. The plant is located in the basement of the main utility building, adjacent to the electrical substation and the STP control room.

The system comprises two (2) water-cooled centrifugal chillers, primary and secondary chilled water pumps, condenser water pumps, cooling towers, and the associated piping, valves, and control instrumentation. This manual covers the technical specifications of the chiller units, their ancillary components, and the recommended maintenance schedule.

**2. SCOPE**

This document is applicable to the operation and maintenance of the CCP equipment listed in Section 3. It is intended for use by the maintenance technicians, shift engineers, and the facilities management team. The specifications provided herein are as per the as-built documentation and the manufacturer’s datasheets. Any deviation from these specifications must be reported to the AGEP Engineering Team.

**3. EQUIPMENT DATASHEET SUMMARY**

The following table provides the salient technical parameters of the chiller units installed in the CCP. The data is as per the original equipment manufacturer’s (OEM) datasheet and the as-built record.

**3.1 Chiller Capacity Specification**

The equipment datasheet for Central Chiller Plant lists its chiller_capacity as 450 TR. Record status: current. This is the rated capacity at the design conditions specified in Table 3.2. This rating is current and is used for all load calculations and performance evaluations for the plant.

**3.2 Design Operating Conditions**

The chillers are designed for the following operating conditions, which are the basis for the capacity rating:

- Chilled water leaving temperature: 7.0°C
- Chilled water entering temperature: 12.0°C
- Condenser water entering temperature: 30.0°C
- Condenser water leaving temperature: 35.5°C
- Fouling factor (evaporator): 0.000018 m²·°C/W
- Fouling factor (condenser): 0.000044 m²·°C/W

**4. COMPRESSOR DETAILS**

Each chiller is fitted with a single-stage centrifugal compressor. The compressor is directly driven by a hermetic electric motor. The motor is cooled by refrigerant injection.

| **Oil Type** | ISO VG 32 (Polyolester – POE) |

| **Speed** | Variable (via VFD) |

The compressor is provided with a variable frequency drive (VFD) for capacity control. The VFD is mounted in the motor control centre (MCC) panel.

| :--- | :--- |

**6.1 Oil Maintenance Procedures**

1.  **Oil Level Check (Weekly):** Check the oil level in the sight glass. The level should be between the 1/2 and 2/3 marks on the sight glass when the compressor is running at full load. If low, add oil through the charging valve. Use only clean, sealed containers of ISO VG 32 POE oil. Do not mix different brands.
2.  **Oil Filter Replacement (Quarterly):** Replace both oil filter elements during the quarterly preventive maintenance. Use only AGEP-approved filter elements (Part No. AGP-OF-32). Before replacement, isolate the oil line and relieve pressure. Record the filter change in the maintenance log.
3.  **Oil Analysis (Yearly or Every 8,000 Running Hours):** Draw a 250 ml oil sample from the sampling valve. Send to an approved laboratory for analysis. Parameters to check: acid number (should be below 0.5 mg KOH/g), moisture content (below 50 ppm), and particle count (ISO 4406 code 17/15/12 or better). If analysis shows contamination or degradation, change the oil.
4.  **Oil Change:** Drain the oil only when the oil is warm (40–50 °C). Dispose of used oil as per local environmental regulations. Refill with fresh oil to the correct level. Run the compressor for 1 hour and re-check the level.

**6.2 Lubrication Chart**

| **Component** | **Lubricant** | **Method** | **Frequency** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Compressor bearings | ISO VG 32 (POE) | Forced feed from oil pump | Continuous |
| Compressor shaft seal | ISO VG 32 (POE) | Forced feed | Continuous |
| VFD cooling fan motor | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, 2 pumps | Semi-annually |
| Condenser water pump bearings | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, until slight purge | Monthly |
| Chilled water pump bearings | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, until slight purge | Monthly |
| Cooling tower fan gearbox | ISO VG 220 (mineral) | Oil level check / top up | Monthly |
| Cooling tower fan motor bearings | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, 2 pumps | Quarterly |
| Actuator linkages (valves) | SAE 30 oil | Light coat on moving parts | Quarterly |

**7. PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE SCHEDULE**

The Preventive Maintenance Schedule (PM Schedule) is the controlling document for all routine maintenance activities on the Central Chiller Plant. The maintenance manual specifies that the Preventive Maintenance Schedule has a pm_frequency of quarterly. Record status: current. This is the current, controlling frequency for all scheduled PM tasks, except where noted otherwise for specific components (e.g., weekly checks, annual oil analysis). This frequency is reviewed annually during the plant shutdown planning, but as of the latest revision (Rev. 04, dated 12-Jan-2025), the quarterly frequency is confirmed as current.

All PM tasks must be performed by trained and authorized maintenance technicians only. Work permits are required for any task involving electrical isolation, refrigerant handling, or working at height. The PM schedule is divided into two main cycles: the Quarterly PM and the Annual PM. The Annual PM includes all Quarterly tasks plus additional in-depth inspections.

**7.1 Quarterly PM – Task Checklist**

The following tasks are to be completed during each quarterly PM. The PM is scheduled for the first full week of January, April, July, and October.
**7.2 Quarterly PM – Task Details**

The following sub-sections describe each task listed in the Quarterly PM checklist. Refer to the relevant section of this manual for detailed procedures, torque values, and safety precautions. All readings must be recorded in the PM log sheet (Form CPL-PM-04).

**7.2.1 Chilled Water Loop Checks**

1.  **Chilled Water Pumps:** Check for unusual noise, vibration, or seal leakage. Record motor running amps and compare with nameplate values. Verify that the pump suction and discharge pressures are within ±5% of the values recorded during the last commissioning test. Grease pump bearings as per the lubrication chart in Section 6.
2.  **Chilled Water Strainers:** Clean the Y-type strainers on the supply and return headers. Inspect the strainer baskets for debris and pitting. If the pressure drop across the strainer exceeds 0.5 kg/cm², the strainer must be cleaned immediately and the cause of fouling investigated.
3.  **Expansion Tank:** Check the water level in the expansion tank and the air bladder pre-charge pressure. The pre-charge pressure should be set to 1.2 kg/cm² (g) when the system is at atmospheric pressure. Top up with nitrogen if required.
4.  **Isolation Valves:** Operate all isolation and balancing valves through one full stroke to ensure they are not seized. Lubricate valve stems with SAE 30 oil as indicated in Section 6. Note any valve that requires excessive force to operate in the PM log.

**7.2.2 Condenser Water Loop Checks**

1.  **Cooling Towers:** Inspect the fill media for scaling, biological growth, and physical damage. Check the drift eliminators for proper seating. Verify that the basin water level is correct and the float valve is operating without sticking.
2.  **Condenser Water Pumps:** Perform the same checks as for chilled water pumps (Section 7.2.1, item 1).
3.  **Water Treatment:** Collect a water sample for analysis as per the water treatment programme. Record the conductivity, pH, and inhibitor residual in the log. The chemical dosing pump must be checked for calibration and proper feed rate.
4.  **Condenser Coil Cleaning:** For air-cooled condensers, inspect the coil fins for dirt, debris, and damage. Clean with low-pressure water or compressed air from the inside out. For water-cooled condensers, refer to the tube cleaning procedure in Section 8.2.

**7.2.3 Refrigerant System Checks**

1.  **Compressor Oil Level:** Check the oil level in the compressor sight glass. The level should be between 1/2 and 3/4 of the sight glass during normal operation. If the level is low, investigate for leaks or oil carryover before topping up.
2.  **Refrigerant Pressure/Temperature:** Record the suction and discharge pressures and temperatures. Compare with the expected values for the current ambient temperature and chilled water setpoint (as per Section 4.2). A deviation of more than 10% warrants further investigation.
3.  **Liquid Line Sight Glass:** Check the sight glass for a solid liquid stream. The presence of bubbles indicates a low refrigerant charge or a restriction in the liquid line.
4.  **Leak Check:** Perform a leak check on all accessible joints, valves, and Schrader ports using an electronic leak detector. Pay special attention to the areas around the compressor shaft seal and the filter-drier.

**7.3 Annual PM – Task Checklist**

The Annual PM is to be scheduled during the long shut down, typically in the month of February. It includes all Quarterly PM tasks plus the following:

**8. TROUBLESHOOTING**

This section provides a guide to common faults, their probable causes, and corrective actions. Always refer to the relevant safety instructions in Section 3 before commencing any troubleshooting activity. The BMS (Building Management System) alarm codes referenced here are the standard codes used by the AGEP BMS interface.
**AGEP Equipment Manuals – Central Chiller Plant Technical Specifications**
**Document No.: AGEP-CP-MAN-004**
**Revision: R3.2**
**Effective Date: 15-11-2023**
**Owner: AGEP Engineering Team**

---

**8. TROUBLESHOOTING (CONTINUED)**

**8.1 BMS Alarm Codes – Quick Reference**

The following table lists the most commonly encountered BMS alarm codes for the central chiller plant. Alarm codes are displayed on the AGEP BMS interface and logged in the plant event recorder. For alarms not listed here, refer to the chiller manufacturer’s controller manual or contact the AGEP helpdesk.

| Alarm Code | Description | Probable Cause | Recommended Action |
|------------|-------------|----------------|--------------------|
| E-101 | Chilled Water Flow Switch Trip | Flow switch faulty, pump not running, or air lock in the line | Verify pump operation and strainer condition. Bleed air from the highest point. Check flow switch setting. |
| E-102 | Condenser Water Flow Switch Trip | Condenser pump failure, clogged strainer, or failed flow switch | Check condenser pump amperage and strainer. Confirm valve positions are fully open. |
| E-103 | Low Chilled Water Temperature | Setpoint too low, sensor drift, or control valve stuck open | Verify setpoint in BMS. Check return and supply temperature sensors against a calibrated thermometer. |
| E-104 | High Condenser Water Temperature | Cooling tower fan failure, fouled condenser tubes, or high ambient conditions | Inspect cooling tower fans and water distribution. Check condenser approach temperature. |
| E-201 | Compressor Overload Trip | High discharge pressure, mechanical binding, or electrical fault | Do not reset more than twice in one hour. Check refrigerant pressures and motor winding resistance. |
| E-202 | Oil Pressure Differential Low | Low oil level, faulty oil pressure switch, or worn oil pump | Check oil level in sight glass. Verify oil pressure transducer reading. |
| E-203 | Refrigerant Low Pressure Trip | Low refrigerant charge, blocked filter-drier, or evaporator fouling | Record suction pressure. Look for frost on the suction line. Leak check the system. |
| E-301 | Starter Fault – Main Compressor | Phase loss, undervoltage, or overload relay trip | Check incoming voltage on all three phases. Inspect contactor and overload relay settings. |
| E-302 | VFD Fault – Primary Pump | VFD overcurrent, heat sink over temperature, or ground fault | Read the VFD fault history. Check motor insulation resistance. Ensure VFD cooling fan is operational. |
| E-401 | BMS Communication Loss | Loose termination, faulty gateway, or controller offline | Check RS-485 wiring and termination resistors. Reboot the gateway. |

**8.2 General Troubleshooting Flow**

1.  **Identify:** Note the alarm code and the time of occurrence from the BMS history log.
2.  **Isolate:** Use the single-line diagram (Drawing No. AGEP-ELD-01) to isolate the affected equipment electrically and mechanically.
3.  **Verify:** Confirm the physical condition of the equipment before changing any settings. A visual inspection often reveals the cause.
4.  **Record:** Log all readings and actions taken in the plant logbook. Do not rely on memory.
5.  **Escalate:** If the fault is not resolved within two hours, or if the same alarm repeats three times in a shift, inform the Shift Engineer and the AGEP helpdesk.

**8.3 Compressor Short-Cycling**

**Symptom:** The compressor starts and stops frequently (more than 6 starts per hour).

**Probable Causes:**
- Low refrigerant charge causing the low-pressure switch to trip.
- Faulty low-pressure switch (cut-out set too high).
- Chilled water flow fluctuation due to a faulty flow switch or a stuck modulating valve.
- Control panel setpoint differential too narrow.

Archive item 5: AGEP Energy Audit Report FY2022-23 – Executive Summary and Consumption Analysis
Source format: Energy Audit Reports

**ARAVALLI GREEN ENERGY PARK**
**ENERGY AUDIT REPORT – FY 2022-23**
**Executive Summary & Consumption Analysis**

**Report No.:** AGEP/EA/2023/05
**Audit Period:** 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2023
**Date of Issue:** 15 June 2023
**Prepared by:** M/s Deshpande Energy Consultants Pvt. Ltd., Jaipur
**Audit Team:** Arjun Deshpande (Lead Auditor), Priya Nair (Energy Analyst), Rohan Mehta (Field Engineer)

---

**1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

This report presents the findings of the comprehensive energy audit conducted at Aravalli Green Energy Park (hereinafter referred to as “the Park” or “AGEP”) for the financial year 2022-23. The audit was commissioned by the Park’s management with the primary objective of assessing the facility’s overall energy performance, identifying significant areas of consumption, and recommending cost-effective measures for energy conservation.

The audit covered all major energy-consuming systems within the Park’s operational boundary, including the administrative buildings, the centralised HVAC plant, the data centre, the common area lighting infrastructure, and the water pumping and treatment systems. The energy audit report FY2022-23 states that Aravalli Green Energy Park's annual_energy_consumption was 3.2 GWh. Record status: historical. This figure, which is considered the official historical baseline for the fiscal year, represents the total purchased electricity from the grid plus the energy generated from the on-site solar PV array that was consumed within the Park’s premises.

Key performance indicators were benchmarked against similar mixed-use business parks in the Rajasthan region. While the Park’s overall energy intensity is comparable to industry norms, the audit identified notable inefficiencies in the HVAC system’s chiller plant operation and in the lighting controls for the basement parking areas. The total identified savings potential is estimated at 3,85,000 kWh per annum, which translates to a financial saving of approximately ₹ 2.4 lakh per year at current tariffs, requiring an estimated capital investment of ₹ 18.5 lakh.

We extend our gratitude to the AGEP facilities team, particularly Mr. Suresh Kumar (Chief Engineer) and Ms. Anjali Sharma (Facility Manager), for their full cooperation and provision of data throughout the audit process.

Arjun Deshpande
Lead Auditor
For M/s Deshpande Energy Consultants Pvt. Ltd.

---

**2. SCOPE OF AUDIT**

The scope of this energy audit was confined to the energy consumption of the entire Aravalli Green Energy Park campus. The specific systems and areas covered are detailed below:

- **Administrative Buildings (Blocks A, B, and C):** Lighting, air conditioning (split and VRV units), office equipment (computers, printers, servers in small server rooms), and lifts.
- **Centralised HVAC Plant:** Chillers, cooling towers, primary and secondary chilled water pumps, condenser water pumps, and Air Handling Units (AHUs) serving the main conference centre and the cafeteria.
- **Data Centre (DC-1):** Dedicated precision cooling units (CRACs), UPS systems, and server loads. This is a high-intensity consumption area.
- **Common Area Infrastructure:** External lighting, internal corridor lighting, lifts in common areas, and signage.
- **Water Systems:** Raw water pumps, sewage treatment plant (STP) blowers and pumps, and horticulture pumping.

The audit did not cover the energy consumption of individual tenants within the Park, as their usage is separately metered and billed by the tenants themselves. The boundary for this audit is the main incoming metering point and the net metering point for the solar PV installation.

---

**3. METHODOLOGY**

The audit was conducted following the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) guidelines and the standard procedures outlined in the relevant Indian Standard (IS) codes. The methodology was structured into four distinct phases:
**3.1 Phase 1: Preliminary Review and Data Collection**

The first phase involved a detailed review of the electrical bills for the entire campus for the period April 2022 to March 2023. Monthly consumption data was collected from the main incoming meter (CT-1) and the solar net meter (CT-2). Additionally, sub-meter readings were collected from the various distribution boards within the administrative blocks, the centralised HVAC plant room, and the data centre. A walk-through survey of the entire campus was conducted during the second week of May 2023 to visually verify the inventory of connected load and to identify obvious instances of energy wastage.

**3.2 Phase 2: Instrumentation and Field Measurements**

During this phase, portable power analysers were connected to the main LT panels of the administrative buildings and the centralised HVAC plant for a period of seven continuous days. The following parameters were recorded at five-minute intervals:

- Voltage (V)
- Current (A) in each phase
- Power factor (PF)
- Active power (kW)
- Reactive power (kVAR)
- Total harmonic distortion (THD) in voltage and current

Spot measurements of illumination levels were taken in various office spaces, the conference centre, and common areas using a lux meter. The measurements were taken during working hours under normal occupancy conditions. Additionally, temperature and humidity readings were logged in the data centre and the main server rooms to assess the performance of the precision cooling units. The performance of the chillers was assessed by measuring the chilled water supply and return temperatures, the condenser water temperatures, and the electrical input power to the compressor. The thermal load on the chillers was calculated based on the chilled water flow rate and the temperature differential.

**3.3 Phase 3: Data Analysis and Benchmarking**

The data collected from the field measurements and the historical billing data were analysed to establish the baseline energy consumption for the campus. The Energy Performance Index (EPI) for the buildings was calculated and compared with benchmarks from the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) and the BEE Star Rating programme for buildings. The performance of the chillers was evaluated in terms of their coefficient of performance (COP) and was compared with the design specifications and the manufacturer's data. The solar PV generation was compared with the expected generation based on the installed capacity and the local solar insolation data.

**3.4 Phase 4: Identification of Energy Conservation Measures and Reporting**

Based on the analysis, a list of potential Energy Conservation Measures (ECMs) was prepared. These measures were evaluated for their technical feasibility, cost, and potential for energy savings. A detailed cost-benefit analysis was carried out for each measure, and the measures were prioritised based on their simple payback period. The findings and recommendations were compiled into this report, which was reviewed by the AGEP management before finalisation.

---

**4. DETAILED FINDINGS AND ANALYSIS**

This section presents the detailed findings of the energy audit for each major system. The findings are based on the data collected during the audit period and the analysis of historical consumption patterns.

**4.1 Electrical Energy Consumption Overview**

The total energy consumption of the campus during FY 2022-23 was recorded at the main incoming meter (CT-1). The monthly consumption data is presented in the table below.

**Table 4.1: Monthly Energy Consumption from Grid (CT-1) – FY 2022-23**

The consumption pattern shows a clear seasonal trend, with the highest consumption occurring during the summer months of May and June, which is primarily attributable to the increased load from the centralised HVAC plant. A secondary peak is also observed in March, likely due to the onset of summer. The maximum demand of 456 kVA was recorded in June 2022.

documents.title: AGEP Operations Handbook – Section 1: Facility Overview and Commissioning
documents.content:
This handbook provides the standard operating procedures, facility specifications, and safety protocols for the Aravalli Green Energy Park (hereafter "AGEP" or "the Park"). It is intended for all AGEP staff, contract personnel, and authorised visitors. Sections are numbered for ease of reference; any conflict between this handbook and a specific work order must be brought to the attention of the Facilities Manager.

**2. FACILITY IDENTIFICATION**

- **Facility Name:** Aravalli Green Energy Park (AGEP)
- **Registered Address:** Plot No. 7, Sector 18, Gurugram – 122015, Haryana, India
- **Land Area:** 12.5 acres
- **Total Built-Up Area:** 18,700 sq. m. (approx.)
- **Number of Main Blocks:** 3 (Admin Block, Operations Block, Maintenance Block)
- **Number of Floors:** Admin Block – 4 floors; Operations Block – 2 floors; Maintenance Block – single storey
- **Primary Function:** Solar energy generation, battery storage, and grid load balancing; also houses the regional dispatch office.

**3. COMMISSIONING RECORD**

The AGEP was formally commissioned on 15-04-2018, following the completion of Phase I construction and the successful run of the Standard Testing Procedure (STP) for all major subsystems. This date is recorded as the official commissioning date in the AGEP Operations Handbook and is used for all warranty, insurance, and statutory compliance calculations.

The commissioning certificate (Ref. No. AGEP/COMM/2018/01) is held in the Facilities Department filing cabinet (Cabinet 2, Drawer A). A copy is also available in the digital archive under "Legal & Compliance".

**4. MAJOR SYSTEMS OVERVIEW**

The AGEP Operations Handbook states that the commissioning_date of Aravalli Green Energy Park is 2018-04-15. Record status: current.

The following systems are critical to the Park's operation. Detailed maintenance schedules are in Section 5 of this handbook.

**4.1 Solar PV Array**
- **Capacity:** 8.5 MWp (DC), 7.2 MW (AC)
- **Module Type:** Monocrystalline, 330 Wp each
- **Inverter Count:** 24 (central string inverters, 300 kW each)
- **Mounting:** Fixed tilt at 24°, south-facing; ground-mounted in rows 1–6.

**4.2 Battery Energy Storage System (BESS)**
- **Capacity:** 10 MWh (lithium-ion)
- **Container Location:** North-east corner, behind Maintenance Block
- **Fire Suppression:** Dedicated aerosol-based system; do not enter BESS area without authorisation.

**4.3 HVAC System**
- **Admin Block:** Two 40 TR variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems; chiller backup of 50 TR.
- **Operations Block:** One 25 TR VRF system.
- **Maintenance Block:** Split AC units (3 units, 1.5 TR each) – not connected to central system.
- **Control Setpoint:** 24°C ± 1°C during occupied hours; 28°C during unoccupied hours (except server room, which is 22°C ± 2°C).

**4.4 Lighting**
- **Type:** LED throughout; 4000K colour temperature in office areas, 5000K in inspection bays.
- **Control:** Occupancy sensors in corridors and restrooms; daylight harvesting in open-plan offices.
- **Emergency Lighting:** Battery-backed units on each floor near stairwells; test weekly (see Section 7.4).

**4.5 Backup Power**
- **Diesel Generators (DG):** 2 × 500 kVA, auto-start on mains failure. One is on standby at all times.
- **Fuel Storage:** 2 × 10,000 litre underground tanks. Fuel quality tested quarterly as per IS 1460.
- **Changeover Time:** < 15 seconds via automatic transfer switch (ATS).

**4.6 Water Systems**
- **Source:** Borewell + municipal supply (dual feed).
- **STP:** On-site sewage treatment plant (STP) of 50 kLD capacity. Treated water used for landscaping and cooling tower make-up.
- **Cooling Tower:** 1 × 100 TR, induced draft, located on Admin Block roof.

**5.0 Daily Operations and Seasonal Adjustments**

The Park operates on a two-shift pattern for core maintenance and security staff, with administrative functions following standard office hours. Shift timings are as follows:

| Shift | Timings | Remarks |
|--------|---------|---------|
| General Shift (Admin) | 09:00 – 18:00 hrs | Monday to Saturday; second Saturday closed |
| Shift A (Operations) | 08:00 – 20:00 hrs | Rotating, 6 days on / 2 days off |
| Shift B (Operations) | 20:00 – 08:00 hrs | Rotating, 6 days on / 2 days off |
| Security | 24 × 7 | Three shifts of 8 hours each |

During Diwali and Holi weeks, the Admin Block follows a reduced schedule (10:00 – 16:00 hrs) unless prior approval is obtained from the Facility Manager for extended hours. The same applies to the week between Christmas and New Year. All leave requests during these periods must be submitted at least 15 days in advance.

**5.1 HVAC Scheduling**

The HVAC systems shall be operated according to the following schedule, which is reviewed quarterly and revised as needed:

| Zone | Occupied Hours | Unoccupied Hours | Notes |
|------|----------------|------------------|-------|
| Admin Block – VRF | 08:30 – 18:30 hrs | 28°C setpoint | Pre-cooling starts at 08:00 hrs |
| Admin Block – Chiller backup | Only when VRF under maintenance or ambient > 38°C | – | Changeover log to be maintained |
| Operations Block – VRF | 07:30 – 20:30 hrs | 28°C setpoint | Shift B has access to local override |
| Server Room (Admin Block) | 24 × 7 | 22°C ± 2°C | Redundant unit; alarm on high temp |
| Maintenance Block – Split Units | As per work requirement | OFF | Units to be switched off when bay is empty |

Seasonal adjustments: From 15 March to 15 October (summer period), the pre-cooling start time is advanced by 30 minutes in the Admin Block. During the monsoon (June to September), the VRF systems in the Operations Block shall be operated in dry mode whenever relative humidity exceeds 80%, as per the manufacturer's recommendation.

The chiller backup shall be started only with the prior approval of the Shift In-charge, and the reason for start-up must be recorded in the HVAC log register. Energy consumption for the chiller is tracked separately under the head "Chiller – Backup".

**5.2 Lighting Control**

Lighting schedules are programmed into the Building Management System (BMS) as follows:

- **Office areas (Admin Block):** 08:00 – 18:30 hrs, with daylight harvesting active. If lux level falls below 300 lux during overcast conditions, the system automatically raises artificial lighting to 50% and then to 100% if required.
- **Corridors and restrooms:** Occupancy sensors; time delay of 10 minutes after last detection.

## 6. SAFETY PROTOCOLS AND EMERGENCY PROCEDURES

### 6.1 General Safety Policy

AGEP is committed to providing a safe working environment for all employees, contractors, and visitors. Every person entering the facility shall comply with the safety rules outlined in this section and with applicable provisions of the Factories Act, 1948, and the Maharashtra Factories Rules, 1963. The Facility Manager is the designated Safety Officer for the premises and shall be responsible for the implementation of this policy.

Safety is everybody's responsibility. Any person noticing an unsafe condition, a potential hazard, or a near-miss incident shall report the same immediately to the Shift In-charge or to the Security Control Room (extension 101). Anonymous reporting is permitted through the suggestion box located near the main entrance gate. Reports received through this channel are reviewed by the Facility Manager on a weekly basis.

All employees shall undergo a safety induction before they are issued access cards. The induction covers fire safety, electrical safety, first aid, and emergency evacuation procedures. Contractors working on-site shall attend a condensed version of this induction, and their supervisor shall sign an acknowledgement confirming that the contractor staff have understood the rules. The Central Chiller Plant (CCP), designated as Asset ENT10 in the campus asset register, is the primary source of chilled water for the air-conditioning system serving the administration block, central library, and the R&D wing. The plant is located in the basement of the main utility building, adjacent to the electrical substation and the STP control room.

The system comprises two (2) water-cooled centrifugal chillers, primary and secondary chilled water pumps, condenser water pumps, cooling towers, and the associated piping, valves, and control instrumentation. This manual covers the technical specifications of the chiller units, their ancillary components, and the recommended maintenance schedule.

**2. SCOPE**

This document is applicable to the operation and maintenance of the CCP equipment listed in Section 3. It is intended for use by the maintenance technicians, shift engineers, and the facilities management team. The specifications provided herein are as per the as-built documentation and the manufacturer’s datasheets. Any deviation from these specifications must be reported to the AGEP Engineering Team.

**6.1 Oil Maintenance Procedures**

1.  **Oil Level Check (Weekly):** Check the oil level in the sight glass. The level should be between the 1/2 and 2/3 marks on the sight glass when the compressor is running at full load. If low, add oil through the charging valve. Use only clean, sealed containers of ISO VG 32 POE oil. Do not mix different brands.
2.  **Oil Filter Replacement (Quarterly):** Replace both oil filter elements during the quarterly preventive maintenance. Use only AGEP-approved filter elements (Part No. AGP-OF-32). Before replacement, isolate the oil line and relieve pressure. Record the filter change in the maintenance log.
3.  **Oil Analysis (Yearly or Every 8,000 Running Hours):** Draw a 250 ml oil sample from the sampling valve. Send to an approved laboratory for analysis. Parameters to check: acid number (should be below 0.5 mg KOH/g), moisture content (below 50 ppm), and particle count (ISO 4406 code 17/15/12 or better). If analysis shows contamination or degradation, change the oil.
4.  **Oil Change:** Drain the oil only when the oil is warm (40–50 °C). Dispose of used oil as per local environmental regulations. Refill with fresh oil to the correct level. Run the compressor for 1 hour and re-check the level.

**6.2 Lubrication Chart**

| **Component** | **Lubricant** | **Method** | **Frequency** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Compressor bearings | ISO VG 32 (POE) | Forced feed from oil pump | Continuous |
| Compressor shaft seal | ISO VG 32 (POE) | Forced feed | Continuous |
| VFD cooling fan motor | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, 2 pumps | Semi-annually |
| Condenser water pump bearings | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, until slight purge | Monthly |
| Chilled water pump bearings | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, until slight purge | Monthly |
| Cooling tower fan gearbox | ISO VG 220 (mineral) | Oil level check / top up | Monthly |
| Cooling tower fan motor bearings | Grease, lithium-based (NLGI 2) | Grease gun, 2 pumps | Quarterly |
| Actuator linkages (valves) | SAE 30 oil | Light coat on moving parts | Quarterly |

**7. PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE SCHEDULE**

The Preventive Maintenance Schedule (PM Schedule) is the controlling document for all routine maintenance activities on the Central Chiller Plant. The maintenance manual specifies that the Preventive Maintenance Schedule has a pm_frequency of quarterly. Record status: current. This is the current, controlling frequency for all scheduled PM tasks, except where noted otherwise for specific components (e.g., weekly checks, annual oil analysis). This frequency is reviewed annually during the plant shutdown planning, but as of the latest revision (Rev. 04, dated 12-Jan-2025), the quarterly frequency is confirmed as current.

All PM tasks must be performed by trained and authorized maintenance technicians only. Work permits are required for any task involving electrical isolation, refrigerant handling, or working at height. The PM schedule is divided into two main cycles: the Quarterly PM and the Annual PM. The Annual PM includes all Quarterly tasks plus additional in-depth inspections.

**7.1 Quarterly PM – Task Checklist**

The following tasks are to be completed during each quarterly PM. The PM is scheduled for the first full week of January, April, July, and October.

**7.2 Quarterly PM – Task Details**

The following sub-sections describe each task listed in the Quarterly PM checklist. Refer to the relevant section of this manual for detailed procedures, torque values, and safety precautions. All readings must be recorded in the PM log sheet (Form CPL-PM-04).

**7.2.1 Chilled Water Loop Checks**

1.  **Chilled Water Pumps:** Check for unusual noise, vibration, or seal leakage. Record motor running amps and compare with nameplate values. Verify that the pump suction and discharge pressures are within ±5% of the values recorded during the last commissioning test. Grease pump bearings as per the lubrication chart in Section 6.
2.  **Chilled Water Strainers:** Clean the Y-type strainers on the supply and return headers. Inspect the strainer baskets for debris and pitting. If the pressure drop across the strainer exceeds 0.5 kg/cm², the strainer must be cleaned immediately and the cause of fouling investigated.
3.  **Expansion Tank:** Check the water level in the expansion tank and the air bladder pre-charge pressure. The pre-charge pressure should be set to 1.2 kg/cm² (g) when the system is at atmospheric pressure. Top up with nitrogen if required.
4.  **Isolation Valves:** Operate all isolation and balancing valves through one full stroke to ensure they are not seized. Lubricate valve stems with SAE 30 oil as indicated in Section 6. Note any valve that requires excessive force to operate in the PM log.

**7.2.2 Condenser Water Loop Checks**

1.  **Cooling Towers:** Inspect the fill media for scaling, biological growth, and physical damage. Check the drift eliminators for proper seating. Verify that the basin water level is correct and the float valve is operating without sticking.
2.  **Condenser Water Pumps:** Perform the same checks as for chilled water pumps (Section 7.2.1, item 1).
3.  **Water Treatment:** Collect a water sample for analysis as per the water treatment programme. Record the conductivity, pH, and inhibitor residual in the log. The chemical dosing pump must be checked for calibration and proper feed rate.
4.  **Condenser Coil Cleaning:** For air-cooled condensers, inspect the coil fins for dirt, debris, and damage. Clean with low-pressure water or compressed air from the inside out. For water-cooled condensers, refer to the tube cleaning procedure in Section 8.2.

**7.2.3 Refrigerant System Checks**

1.  **Compressor Oil Level:** Check the oil level in the compressor sight glass. The level should be between 1/2 and 3/4 of the sight glass during normal operation. If the level is low, investigate for leaks or oil carryover before topping up.
2.  **Refrigerant Pressure/Temperature:** Record the suction and discharge pressures and temperatures. Compare with the expected values for the current ambient temperature and chilled water setpoint (as per Section 4.2). A deviation of more than 10% warrants further investigation.
3.  **Liquid Line Sight Glass:** Check the sight glass for a solid liquid stream. The presence of bubbles indicates a low refrigerant charge or a restriction in the liquid line.
4.  **Leak Check:** Perform a leak check on all accessible joints, valves, and Schrader ports using an electronic leak detector. Pay special attention to the areas around the compressor shaft seal and the filter-drier.

**7.3 Annual PM – Task Checklist**

The Annual PM is to be scheduled during the long shut down, typically in the month of February. It includes all Quarterly PM tasks plus the following:

**8. TROUBLESHOOTING**

This section provides a guide to common faults, their probable causes, and corrective actions. Always refer to the relevant safety instructions in Section 3 before commencing any troubleshooting activity. The BMS (Building Management System) alarm codes referenced here are the standard codes used by the AGEP BMS interface.

**8. TROUBLESHOOTING (CONTINUED)**

**8.1 BMS Alarm Codes – Quick Reference**

The following table lists the most commonly encountered BMS alarm codes for the central chiller plant. Alarm codes are displayed on the AGEP BMS interface and logged in the plant event recorder. For alarms not listed here, refer to the chiller manufacturer’s controller manual or contact the AGEP helpdesk.

| Alarm Code | Description | Probable Cause | Recommended Action |
|------------|-------------|----------------|--------------------|
| E-101 | Chilled Water Flow Switch Trip | Flow switch faulty, pump not running, or air lock in the line | Verify pump operation and strainer condition. Bleed air from the highest point. Check flow switch setting. |
| E-102 | Condenser Water Flow Switch Trip | Condenser pump failure, clogged strainer, or failed flow switch | Check condenser pump amperage and strainer. Confirm valve positions are fully open. |
| E-103 | Low Chilled Water Temperature | Setpoint too low, sensor drift, or control valve stuck open | Verify setpoint in BMS. Check return and supply temperature sensors against a calibrated thermometer. |
| E-104 | High Condenser Water Temperature | Cooling tower fan failure, fouled condenser tubes, or high ambient conditions | Inspect cooling tower fans and water distribution. Check condenser approach temperature. |
| E-201 | Compressor Overload Trip | High discharge pressure, mechanical binding, or electrical fault | Do not reset more than twice in one hour. Check refrigerant pressures and motor winding resistance. |
| E-202 | Oil Pressure Differential Low | Low oil level, faulty oil pressure switch, or worn oil pump | Check oil level in sight glass. Verify oil pressure transducer reading. |
| E-203 | Refrigerant Low Pressure Trip | Low refrigerant charge, blocked filter-drier, or evaporator fouling | Record suction pressure. Look for frost on the suction line. Leak check the system. |
| E-301 | Starter Fault – Main Compressor | Phase loss, undervoltage, or overload relay trip | Check incoming voltage on all three phases. Inspect contactor and overload relay settings. |
| E-302 | VFD Fault – Primary Pump | VFD overcurrent, heat sink over temperature, or ground fault | Read the VFD fault history. Check motor insulation resistance. Ensure VFD cooling fan is operational. |
| E-401 | BMS Communication Loss | Loose termination, faulty gateway, or controller offline | Check RS-485 wiring and termination resistors. Reboot the gateway. |

**8.2 General Troubleshooting Flow**

1.  **Identify:** Note the alarm code and the time of occurrence from the BMS history log.
2.  **Isolate:** Use the single-line diagram (Drawing No. AGEP-ELD-01) to isolate the affected equipment electrically and mechanically.
3.  **Verify:** Confirm the physical condition of the equipment before changing any settings. A visual inspection often reveals the cause.
4.  **Record:** Log all readings and actions taken in the plant logbook. Do not rely on memory.
5.  **Escalate:** If the fault is not resolved within two hours, or if the same alarm repeats three times in a shift, inform the Shift Engineer and the AGEP helpdesk.

**8.3 Compressor Short-Cycling**

**Symptom:** The compressor starts and stops frequently (more than 6 starts per hour).

**Probable Causes:**
- Low refrigerant charge causing the low-pressure switch to trip.
- Faulty low-pressure switch (cut-out set too high).
- Chilled water flow fluctuation due to a faulty flow switch or a stuck modulating valve.
- Control panel setpoint differential too narrow.

documents.content:
**ARAVALLI GREEN ENERGY PARK**
**ENERGY AUDIT REPORT – FY 2022-23**
**Executive Summary & Consumption Analysis**

**Report No.:** AGEP/EA/2023/05
**Audit Period:** 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2023
**Date of Issue:** 15 June 2023
**Prepared by:** M/s Deshpande Energy Consultants Pvt. Ltd., Jaipur
**Audit Team:** Arjun Deshpande (Lead Auditor), Priya Nair (Energy Analyst), Rohan Mehta (Field Engineer)

---

**1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

This report presents the findings of the comprehensive energy audit conducted at Aravalli Green Energy Park (hereinafter referred to as “the Park” or “AGEP”) for the financial year 2022-23. The audit was commissioned by the Park’s management with the primary objective of assessing the facility’s overall energy performance, identifying significant areas of consumption, and recommending cost-effective measures for energy conservation.

The audit covered all major energy-consuming systems within the Park’s operational boundary, including the administrative buildings, the centralised HVAC plant, the data centre, the common area lighting infrastructure, and the water pumping and treatment systems. The energy audit report FY2022-23 states that Aravalli Green Energy Park's annual_energy_consumption was 3.2 GWh. Record status: historical. This figure, which is considered the official historical baseline for the fiscal year, represents the total purchased electricity from the grid plus the energy generated from the on-site solar PV array that was consumed within the Park’s premises.

Key performance indicators were benchmarked against similar mixed-use business parks in the Rajasthan region. While the Park’s overall energy intensity is comparable to industry norms, the audit identified notable inefficiencies in the HVAC system’s chiller plant operation and in the lighting controls for the basement parking areas. The total identified savings potential is estimated at 3,85,000 kWh per annum, which translates to a financial saving of approximately ₹ 2.4 lakh per year at current tariffs, requiring an estimated capital investment of ₹ 18.5 lakh.

We extend our gratitude to the AGEP facilities team, particularly Mr. Suresh Kumar (Chief Engineer) and Ms. Anjali Sharma (Facility Manager), for their full cooperation and provision of data throughout the audit process.

Arjun Deshpande
Lead Auditor
For M/s Deshpande Energy Consultants Pvt. Ltd.

---

**2. SCOPE OF AUDIT**

The scope of this energy audit was confined to the energy consumption of the entire Aravalli Green Energy Park campus. The specific systems and areas covered are detailed below:

- **Administrative Buildings (Blocks A, B, and C):** Lighting, air conditioning (split and VRV units), office equipment (computers, printers, servers in small server rooms), and lifts.
- **Centralised HVAC Plant:** Chillers, cooling towers, primary and secondary chilled water pumps, condenser water pumps, and Air Handling Units (AHUs) serving the main conference centre and the cafeteria.
- **Data Centre (DC-1):** Dedicated precision cooling units (CRACs), UPS systems, and server loads. This is a high-intensity consumption area.
- **Common Area Infrastructure:** External lighting, internal corridor lighting, lifts in common areas, and signage.
- **Water Systems:** Raw water pumps, sewage treatment plant (STP) blowers and pumps, and horticulture pumping.

The audit did not cover the energy consumption of individual tenants within the Park, as their usage is separately metered and billed by the tenants themselves. The boundary for this audit is the main incoming metering point and the net metering point for the solar PV installation.

---

**3. METHODOLOGY**

The audit was conducted following the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) guidelines and the standard procedures outlined in the relevant Indian Standard (IS) codes. The methodology was structured into four distinct phases:

documents.title: AGEP Energy Audit Report FY2022-23 – Executive Summary and Consumption Analysis
documents.content:
**3.1 Phase 1: Preliminary Review and Data Collection**

The first phase involved a detailed review of the electrical bills for the entire campus for the period April 2022 to March 2023. Monthly consumption data was collected from the main incoming meter (CT-1) and the solar net meter (CT-2). Additionally, sub-meter readings were collected from the various distribution boards within the administrative blocks, the centralised HVAC plant room, and the data centre. A walk-through survey of the entire campus was conducted during the second week of May 2023 to visually verify the inventory of connected load and to identify obvious instances of energy wastage.

**3.2 Phase 2: Instrumentation and Field Measurements**

During this phase, portable power analysers were connected to the main LT panels of the administrative buildings and the centralised HVAC plant for a period of seven continuous days. The following parameters were recorded at five-minute intervals:

- Voltage (V)
- Current (A) in each phase
- Power factor (PF)
- Active power (kW)
- Reactive power (kVAR)
- Total harmonic distortion (THD) in voltage and current

Spot measurements of illumination levels were taken in various office spaces, the conference centre, and common areas using a lux meter. The measurements were taken during working hours under normal occupancy conditions. Additionally, temperature and humidity readings were logged in the data centre and the main server rooms to assess the performance of the precision cooling units. The performance of the chillers was assessed by measuring the chilled water supply and return temperatures, the condenser water temperatures, and the electrical input power to the compressor. The thermal load on the chillers was calculated based on the chilled water flow rate and the temperature differential.

**3.3 Phase 3: Data Analysis and Benchmarking**

The data collected from the field measurements and the historical billing data were analysed to establish the baseline energy consumption for the campus. The Energy Performance Index (EPI) for the buildings was calculated and compared with benchmarks from the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) and the BEE Star Rating programme for buildings. The performance of the chillers was evaluated in terms of their coefficient of performance (COP) and was compared with the design specifications and the manufacturer's data. The solar PV generation was compared with the expected generation based on the installed capacity and the local solar insolation data.

**3.4 Phase 4: Identification of Energy Conservation Measures and Reporting**

Based on the analysis, a list of potential Energy Conservation Measures (ECMs) was prepared. These measures were evaluated for their technical feasibility, cost, and potential for energy savings. A detailed cost-benefit analysis was carried out for each measure, and the measures were prioritised based on their simple payback period. The findings and recommendations were compiled into this report, which was reviewed by the AGEP management before finalisation.

---

**4. DETAILED FINDINGS AND ANALYSIS**

This section presents the detailed findings of the energy audit for each major system. The findings are based on the data collected during the audit period and the analysis of historical consumption patterns.

**4.1 Electrical Energy Consumption Overview**

The total energy consumption of the campus during FY 2022-23 was recorded at the main incoming meter (CT-1). The monthly consumption data is presented in the table below.

**Table 4.1: Monthly Energy Consumption from Grid (CT-1) – FY 2022-23**

The consumption pattern shows a clear seasonal trend, with the highest consumption occurring during the summer months of May and June, which is primarily attributable to the increased load from the centralised HVAC plant. A secondary peak is also observed in March, likely due to the onset of summer. The maximum demand of 456 kVA was recorded in June 2022.
